item.title: State-Space-Based FIR Filtering on a Quantum Computer
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Realizes bounded finite impulse response (FIR) filtering on a quantum computer via a unitary state-space lattice decomposition without mid-circuit measurements or gain loss, demonstrated on N=32 samples with filter order M=12.

Grade 0.470 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Roope Salmi, Davide Rocchesso, Vesa Välimäki

Figure

Sample index n versus normalized amplitude for two parallel input signals (impulse x0(n) and fractal sequence x1(n), red) and their resulting lowpass filtered outputs (y0(n) and y1(n), blue), comparing exact statevector amplitudes with 1024-shot Hadamard test estimates.

Asks

How can discrete-time sample-based linear signal processing and FIR filters be implemented in a composable unitary quantum circuit without losing signal gain?

Before

In prior quantum FIR filters (Majumdar et al. 2021), input samples were consumed without reuse, preventing composability without intermediate classical conversion.

But

Simulated on ideal quantum simulator with 1024-shot sampling; requires known power complementary transfer function and large circuit depths (59,292 elementary gates for N=32,M=12) requiring fault-tolerant hardware.

Tools

Vaidyanathan unitary lattice filterbank decomposition · quantum delay and transposition gates · Hadamard test · Qiskit simulator

Code. https://github.com/ollpu/quantum-fir/

Abstract

Many signal processing tasks require intensive computations. Quantum computing promises to accelerate certain tasks, but algorithms must be designed around the limitations of quantum mechanics. This paper provides a quantum implementation of finite impulse response (FIR) filters, which are a widely used tool in classical signal processing. The filter can be parallelized and composed as part of larger quantum algorithms, with potential for speedups using quantum amplitude estimation and future fault-tolerant quantum hardware. To accomplish these properties, we introduce a state-space framework wherein sample-based signal processing is performed with unitary quantum circuits. We present the quantum delay gate as the quantum analog of the delay line in discrete-time signal processing. Unitary circuits intrinsically describe lossless systems, but we also implement lowpass and other bounded filters by emulating a projection operator. The FIR filter implementation is tested and demonstrated with a quantum circuit simulator.

item.title: Blind Quantum Computation with a Small Quantum Server
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Constructed blind quantum computation (Blind PBC) requiring a quantum server of only t qubits for an n-qubit circuit with t non-Clifford T gates, achieving perfect information-theoretic input secrecy with four-way random state preparation and a single t-qubit quantum communication step.

Grade 0.423 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “dequantization and classical algorithms that match quantum claims” · Daniel Lovsted, Filipa C. R. Peres, Joshua Nevin, Selman Ipek, Anne Broadbent

Figure

Comparison of standard Pauli-based computation (a) with Blind PBC (b), illustrating state preparation with client random phase rotations SciZdi, adaptive Pauli observable measurement via client-side circuit modification 𝖯𝖡𝖢.𝖲𝖾𝗅(C𝐱∗), and output sample decoding.

Asks

How can blind quantum computation be performed while minimizing the required quantum processor size on the server?

Before

Server size was n+t qubits for single-instance communication or n+1 qubits with t sequential communication rounds in quantum computing on encrypted data (QCED).

But

Hides computational basis input 𝐱 (or orthonormal stabilizer bases) but reveals circuit structure C. Qubit virtualization incurs classical sampling cost exponential in simulated virtual qubit count k.

Tools

Pauli-based computation (PBC) · Magic state teleportation gadgets · One-way four-phase quantum state encryption · Tailored resource computation (TRC)

Abstract

Blind quantum computation (BQC) allows low-resource clients to securely delegate computations to a quantum server, but server resource costs scale with the computation size, posing a bottleneck for implementations. By leveraging Pauli-based computation (PBC), we achieve BQC with a server whose size depends only on the non-Clifford gate count. Our protocol inherits fault tolerance and qubit virtualization from PBC and reveals that classical-client BQC is possible even in the absence of classical simulability. Finally, we present an entanglement-based dual protocol that performs a resource state computation with a dramatically reduced execution cost.

item.title: Quantum computers will not be that different: A blueprint for quantum computer architecture at scale
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Defines architectural blueprint for utility-scale quantum-classical systems using standard classical accelerator and high-performance network stack principles, organizing low-level control, readout, and quantum error correction below an instruction set architecture abstraction boundary.

Grade 0.421 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Torsten Hoefler, Matthias Troyer

Asks

How should utility-scale quantum computer architectures be structured across coupled quantum-classical systems to optimize cost-performance?

But

Conceptual architectural blueprint rather than empirical hardware implementation.

Tools

Instruction set architecture (ISA) abstraction · High-performance networking paradigms · Hardware-specialized QEC decoders · Heterogeneous accelerator design

Abstract

Quantum computers are technologically novel and unusual, but at system scale they should be engineered using many of the same principles that govern classical heterogeneous accelerators. This paper argues that utility-scale quantum architecture is primarily a cost-performance problem across a coupled quantum-classical system, leading to a blueprint for scalable quantum processing unit (QPU) design. Our architecture blueprint is organized around clean logical abstractions, hiding details and complexity of physical qubit modalities below the instruction set architecture (ISA) boundary, and specializes recurring functions aggressively to minimize the cost for utility scale quantum computations. Its low-level implementation through specialized local hardware for control, readout, and quantum error correction (QEC) closely resembles the architecture of high-performance network stacks. One of our main insights is that the design principles and the resulting architecture closely follow established practice from classical computing and networking.

item.title: Quantum WalkScore: Benchmarking Quantum Computers on the Graph Nodefinding Problem
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Defines Quantum WalkScore (QWS), an application-oriented benchmark quantifying the largest problem size (n,d) on cycle and 2D-torus graphs where discrete-time quantum walks with amplitude amplification find a target node with measured success probability pexp(n,d)≥p∗(n,d) before first failure.

Grade 0.418 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Noé Olivier, Michel Nowak

Figure

Cycle and 2D-torus graph structures for nodefinding instances of sizes n=4 and n=3 with target nodes located at varied distances d from the source.

Asks

How can discrete-time quantum walks combined with amplitude amplification benchmark quantum computers on graph search problems?

But

Applies to gate-based quantum computers on cycle and 2D-torus graphs; walk step counts require 𝗇𝗎𝗆-𝗐≥d and 𝗇𝗎𝗆-𝗐≡d(mod2).

Tools

Discrete-time quantum walks (DTQW) · Quantum amplitude amplification (AA) · IBM Heron r2, Heron r3, and Nighthawk r1 QPUs · Noiseless quantum circuit simulation

Abstract

Recent advances in quantum computing hardware toward fault-tolerance have increased interest in evaluating near-term quantum platforms on application-relevant quantum algorithms. In this work, we introduce Quantum WalkScore (QWS), a scalable application-oriented benchmark designed to assess the performance of NISQ and future fault-tolerant quantum computers in executing essential quantum routines --discrete-time quantum walks and quantum amplitude amplification-- to solve the graph nodefinding problem (marked-vertex search). QWS quantifies performance by scoring the largest problem size for which a designated target node can be found with success probability above a defined threshold. In addition to the complete protocol description, we provide example parameter-selection scenarios designed from noiseless simulation results and demonstrate QWS evaluation through experimental runs on multiple generations of IBM real quantum processors.

item.title: Linear combination of Schrödingerization for quantum linear systems with optimal matrix-query complexity
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Constructed an ODE-based QLSA reaching optimal matrix-query and RHS-query complexity 𝒪(κAlog⁡(1/ε)) without variable-time amplitude amplification (VTAA).

Grade 0.411 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations” · Yin Yang, Yue Yu, Long Zhang

Figure

Quantum circuit schematic executing the two-level LCHS routine with interval marking OI and flag verification.

Asks

Can quantum linear systems be solved with optimal query complexity 𝒪(κlog⁡(1/ε)) using an ODE/Schrödingerization framework without requiring variable-time amplitude amplification?

Before

LCU+VTAA (Childs et al. 2017) had query complexity 𝒪(κpolylog⁡(κ/ε)).

But

Requires auxiliary-state preparation oracles and a constant-factor estimate of the solution norm. Gate-level compilation and implementation not provided.

Tools

LC-Schrödingerization · Two-level LCHS · Gaussian-smoothed hat kernel · Auxiliary interval recovery · Block preconditioning

Abstract

Quantum linear systems algorithms (QLSAs) aim to solve linear systems Abbx=bbb exponentially faster than classical methods under certain conditions. In this work, we develop quantum algorithms for solving linear algebraic equations from an ODE-based perspective. Inspired by the linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation (LCHS) representation in the Fourier approach citeChilds2017QLSA, we express the solution bbx as a linear combination of solutions to a system of linear convection equations, which become Schrödinger-type equations with unitary evolutions in the Fourier domain. We refer to this representation as LC-Schrödingerization. Based on this result, we construct an LCHS-based quantum algorithm with two LCHS instances: one for time-marching and one for numerical integration. The key construction uses the derivative of a Gaussian-smoothed hat function and recovers the solution over a fixed auxiliary interval. This permits a truncation time independent of the target accuracy and avoids the loss in success probability from selecting a single grid point. Periodization and explicit Fourier coefficients provide the corresponding projection error bounds. Under the stated oracle assumptions and given a constant-factor estimate of the solution norm, direct simulation of the select operators and block preconditioning achieve the optimal matrix-query complexity O(κ_Alogfrac1ε) without using variable-time amplitude amplification (VTAA). The same upper bound holds for queries to the right-hand-side preparation oracle.

item.title: Hardness of Pathfinding in a Welded Tree
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Finding a path from entrance to exit in a welded tree of height n requires at least Ω(2n/24) quantum queries (or Ω(N1/24)) to succeed with constant probability.

Grade 0.406 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · David Miloschewsky, Supartha Podder

Figure

Schematic of the fresh compressed oracle rule restricting weld query assignments. Gray nodes mark visited database records, green nodes are valid fresh connections, and red nodes are forbidden to prevent cycles or premature component joining.

Asks

Does there exist an efficient quantum algorithm that outputs a path between the entrance and exit vertices of a welded tree?

Before

Childs, Coudron, and Gilani (CCG23) proved pathfinding hardness restricted to rooted and genuine quantum algorithms, but general quantum algorithms remained open.

But

Welded tree graphs of height n (N=2n leaves) with q≤N/100 queries and a single-cycle weld distribution with fixed edge colorings.

Tools

compressed permutation oracles · fresh compressed oracle framework · quantum discrete walk column-direction states

Abstract

Starting from the entrance of a welded tree, a quantum walk algorithm can find its exit vertex exponentially faster than any classical algorithm. However, it has been an open question whether any quantum algorithm is able to efficiently find a path from the entrance to the exit. We answer this by proving an exponential quantum query lower bound for finding such path. Specifically, for trees of height n, any quantum query algorithm requires at least Ω(2^(n/24)) queries in order to succeed with constant probability. Our proof uses the compressed permutation oracle technique in order to construct databases which track the graph information an algorithm has learned and forgotten, and show that no efficient quantum algorithm can build an entrance-to-exit path in these records.

item.title: The effects of shot noise on the quantum computation of NMR spectra
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — The number of quantum measurement shots required to reconstruct NMR spectra at fixed accuracy scales sub-exponentially with spin-chain length L, showing a pronounced flattening for 1D and 2D molecular geometries with distance-decaying couplings up to L=50.

Grade 0.404 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Sebastian Walch, Keith R. Fratus, Jan-Michael Reiner, Igor Lesanovsky

Figure

Spectral infidelity versus system size L (at R=1024 shots) for 1D chains and four real molecules under full Heisenberg interactions, demonstrating weak growth with L.

Asks

How does the number of projective measurement shots required to compute NMR spectra to a given accuracy scale with the number of nuclear spins?

But

Low-field NMR setting only. All gate noise, decoherence, and Trotterization errors neglected (pure shot-noise limit). Full Heisenberg dynamics verified only up to L=12 and on four real molecules.

Tools

Exact diagonalization · Ising NMR toy Hamiltonian benchmark · Repeated-measurement shot-noise simulation · Fast Fourier transform (FFT)

Abstract

Recent advances in the field of quantum computing hardware motivate the search for applications which demonstrate so-called quantum advantage. One promising use case that has been identified is the simulation of quantum many-body systems. The computational resources required for performing such a simulation on a classical computer generally grow exponentially with the size of the system being modeled, which is ultimately due to the exponential growth of the Hilbert space in which the dynamics of such a system take place. While digital quantum computers natively evolve quantum states directly in such a Hilbert space, thus naively avoiding this problem, the result of such a computation is typically not obtained as a deterministic output. Rather, it requires projective measurements which are fundamentally affected by shot noise. Any desired expectation values must therefore be reconstructed from repeated measurements, making the number of those measurements a relevant computational resource, and thus an important consideration for any potential claims of quantum advantage. In this work, we study how this resource scales with system size (a scaling which itself depends on the desired accuracy of the final result), using the simulation of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra as a test case. We study this scaling for both real-world molecules, as well as a class of model NMR Hamiltonians which allow for efficient large-scale simulations with one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and all-to-all interactions. We find that the required resources increase only weakly with molecular size, far below the exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space. This result suggests that shot noise should not pose a fundamental barrier to achieving quantum advantage in the simulation of NMR systems, and perhaps for many-body systems more broadly.

One promising use case that has been identified is the simulation of quantum many-body systems. The computational resources required for performing such a simulation on a classical computer generally grow exponentially with the size of the system being modeled, which is ultimately due to the exponential growth of the Hilbert space in which the dynamics of such a system take place. While digital quantum computers natively evolve quantum states directly in such a Hilbert space, thus naively avoiding this problem, the result of such a computation is typically not obtained as a deterministic output. Rather, it requires projective measurements which are fundamentally affected by shot noise. Any desired expectation values must therefore be reconstructed from repeated measurements, making the number of those measurements a relevant computational resource, and thus an important consideration for any potential claims of quantum advantage. In this work, we study how this resource scales with system size (a scaling which itself depends on the desired accuracy of the final result), using the simulation of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra as a test case. We study this scaling for both real-world molecules, as well as a class of model NMR Hamiltonians which allow for efficient large-scale simulations with one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and all-to-all interactions. We find that the required resources increase only weakly with molecular size, far below the exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space. This result suggests that shot noise should not pose a fundamental barrier to achieving quantum advantage in the simulation of NMR systems, and perhaps for many-body systems more broadly.

item.title: QECirc: A Community-Driven, FAIR Library of Quantum Error Correction Circuits
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Created QECirc (qecirc.com), an open, verified library providing standardized Stim and OpenQASM implementations for quantum error correction circuits spanning encoders, state preparation, and logical gates.

Grade 0.379 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Ludwig Schmid, Tom Peham, Robert Wille

Asks

How can quantum error correction circuits scattered across papers and ad-hoc repositories be standardized, verified, and made interoperable?

Before

Error Correction Zoo catalogs QEC code properties, but lacks concrete, format-agnostic implementation circuits.

But

Syndrome-extraction schedules and larger qLDPC code families such as bivariate-bicycle codes remain planned work.

Tools

QECirc · Stim · OpenQASM · Crumble · Quirk

Abstract

Quantum error correction (QEC) underpins fault-tolerant quantum computing, but the circuits that realize QEC codes (encoders, logical state-preparation and gate routines, and syndrome-extraction schedules) are scattered across papers and one-off repositories in incompatible formats, often documented too sparsely to reconstruct or reuse. We present QECirc (https://qecirc.com/), a community-driven, open library that makes QEC circuits Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR). Each entry links to its underlying code, ships in Stim and OpenQASM with interactive visualizations, and is checked for correctness before publication. In short, where a catalog such as the Error Correction Zoo describes the codes, QECirc provides the concrete circuits that realize them.
